questions.question:
Choose the correct answer (Any twenty):

i) ________ is a pile in which items are added at one end and removed from the other.
(a) List (b) Queue (c) Stack (d) Array

ii) Which of the following is non-linear data structure?
(a) Trees (b) Stacks (c) Strings (d) All of the above

iii) ________ is not the operation that can be performed on queue.
(a) Traversal (b) Insertion (c) Deletion (d) Retrieval

iv) Which is/are the application(s) of stack?
(a) Function calls (b) Large number Arithmetic (c) Evaluation of arithmetic expressions (d) All of the above

v) Which of the following data structures are indexed structures?
(a) Stack (b) Linked lists (c) Linear arrays (d) None of the above

vi) Linear arrays are also called -
(a) One-dimensional array (b) Vertical array (c) Horizontal array (d) All of the above

vii) Binary trees with threads are called as -
(a) Special trees (b) Pointer trees (c) Threaded trees (d) None of the above

viii) In Binary trees nodes with no successor are called -
(a) End nodes (b) Final nodes (c) Last nodes (d) Terminal nodes

ix) The depth Dn of a complete binary tree of n nodes given by -
(a) Dn = n log₂ n (b) Dn = n log₂(n+1) (c) Dn = log₂ n (d) Dn = log₂(n+1)

x) Every node N in a binary tree T except the root has a unique parent called the ________ of N.
(a) Predecessor (b) Antecedents (c) Precursor (d) None of the above

xi) The in-order traversal of tree will yield a sorted listing of elements of tree in ________.
(a) Merging (b) AVL Trees (c) Binary trees (d) Binary search trees

xii) The post-order traversal of a binary tree is DEBFCA. Find out the pre-order traversal -
(a) ABFCDE (b) ADBFEC (c) ABDECF (d) ABDCEF

xiii) Three standards ways of traversing a binary tree T with root R -
(a) Prefix, infix, postfix (b) Pre-process, in-process, post-process (c) Pre-traversal, in-traversal, post-traversal (d) Pre-order, in-order, post-order

xiv) A full binary tree with n leaves contains -
(a) n - 1 nodes (b) log₂ n nodes (c) 2n - 1 nodes (d) 2ⁿ nodes

xv) The smallest element of an array's index is called its -
(a) extraction (b) range (c) lower bound (d) upper bound

xvi) The data structure required for Breadth First Search on a graph is -
(a) queue (b) stack (c) array (d) None of the above

xvii) The data structure required to evaluate a postfix expression is -
(a) queue (b) stack (c) linked-list (d) All of the above

xviii) The postfix form of AB + C/D is -
(a) ABCD+/ (b) ABCD/+ (c) AB/CD+ (d) A*BC+/D

xix) A linear collection of data elements where the linear node is given by means of pointer is called -
(a) Linked list (b) node list (c) primitive list (d) None of these

xx) Representation of data structure in memory is known as -
(a) Storage structure (b) file structure (c) abstract data type (d) None of the above

xxi) For an undirected graph with n vertices and e edges, the sum of the degree of each vertex is equal to -
(a) 2n (b) 2e (c) (e²+1)/2 (d) (2n-1)/2

xxii) Which of the following data structure is nonlinear type?
(a) Graph (b) Stacks (c) Lists (d) None of the above

xxiii) When new data are to be inserted into a data structure, but there is not available space; this situation is usually called -
(a) Overflow (b) Underflow (c) houseful (d) memory full

xxiv) A data structure where elements can be added or removed at either end but not in the middle is called -
(a) Stacks (b) queues (c) dequeue (d) linked lists

xxv) Which of the following is not the type of queue?
(a) Priority queue (b) Circular queue (c) Ordinary queue (d) Single ended queue
questions.answer:
i) (b) Queue
Explanation: A Queue is a pile (linear structure) where items are added at one end (REAR) and removed from the other end (FRONT) — following FIFO principle.

ii) (a) Trees
Explanation: Trees are non-linear data structures because elements are arranged in a hierarchical (multi-level) manner, not in a single sequence. Stacks and Strings are linear.

iii) (a) Traversal
Explanation: Standard queue operations are Insertion (Enqueue), Deletion (Dequeue), and Retrieval (accessing front element). Traversal is not a standard queue operation — queues are accessed only at front and rear.

iv) (d) All of the above
Explanation: Stack is used for:
- Function calls (call stack management)
- Large number arithmetic
- Evaluation of arithmetic expressions (postfix evaluation)

v) (c) Linear arrays
Explanation: Linear arrays are indexed structures because each element can be directly accessed using its index number. Stacks and Linked lists do not support direct index-based access.

vi) (a) One-dimensional array
Explanation: A linear array stores elements in a single row (one dimension), so it is also called a one-dimensional array.

vii) (c) Threaded trees
Explanation: A binary tree in which NULL pointers are replaced by threads (pointers to in-order predecessor or successor) is called a Threaded Binary Tree.

viii) (d) Terminal nodes
Explanation: Nodes in a binary tree that have no successors (no children) are called terminal nodes, also known as leaf nodes.

ix) (c) Dn = log₂ n
Explanation: The depth (height) of a complete binary tree with n nodes is floor(log₂ n). This is because each level doubles the number of nodes.

x) (d) None of the above
Explanation: The unique node directly above node N in a binary tree is called the PARENT of N. None of the given options (Predecessor, Antecedents, Precursor) correctly describes this relationship.

xi) (d) Binary search trees
Explanation: Inorder traversal (Left → Root → Right) of a Binary Search Tree yields elements in sorted ascending order, because of the BST property (left < root < right).

xii) (c) ABDECF
Explanation: Post-order is DEBFCA. In post-order, root is always the LAST element → Root = A.
Left subtree post-order: DEBF (pre-order will be traversed as B first, then left=D, then right=EF... giving ABD...)
Working backwards: Pre-order = ABDECF.

xiii) (d) Pre-order, in-order, post-order
Explanation: The three standard ways of traversing a binary tree are:
- Pre-order: Root → Left → Right
- In-order: Left → Root → Right
- Post-order: Left → Right → Root

xiv) (c) 2n - 1 nodes
Explanation: A full binary tree with n leaf nodes has a total of 2n - 1 nodes (n leaves + n-1 internal nodes). This follows from the property: L = I + 1, so total = L + I = n + (n-1) = 2n-1.

xv) (c) lower bound
Explanation: The smallest (minimum) index of an array is called its lower bound. For a C array, lower bound = 0. Upper bound is the largest index.

xvi) (a) queue
Explanation: BFS (Breadth First Search) uses a Queue to explore nodes level by level. Nodes are enqueued when discovered and dequeued when visited.

xvii) (b) stack
Explanation: A Stack is used to evaluate postfix expressions. Operands are pushed; when an operator is encountered, two operands are popped, operation is performed, and result is pushed back.

xviii) (b) ABCD/+
Explanation: Convert AB + C/D to postfix:
AB + C/D:
C/D → CD/ (postfix of C/D)
AB + CD/ → AB+CD/ ... 
Correct postfix: AB C D / +
Answer: (b) ABCD/+

xix) (a) Linked list
Explanation: A linked list is a linear collection of data elements (nodes) where each node contains data and a pointer to the next node — the linear order is given by means of pointers.

xx) (a) Storage structure
Explanation: The representation (or implementation) of a data structure in the computer's memory is called a storage structure. It describes how data is physically stored.

xxi) (b) 2e
Explanation: For an undirected graph with e edges, each edge contributes 2 to the total degree sum (one for each endpoint). Therefore, sum of degrees of all vertices = 2e. This is the Handshaking Lemma.

xxii) (a) Graph
Explanation: Graph is a non-linear data structure where nodes (vertices) are connected by edges and can have complex many-to-many relationships. Stacks and Lists are linear.

xxiii) (a) Overflow
Explanation: When new data is to be inserted into a data structure but no space is available, it is called Overflow. Underflow is the opposite — when deletion is attempted on an empty structure.

xxiv) (c) dequeue
Explanation: A Deque (Double Ended Queue) allows insertion and deletion at both ends (front and rear) but not in the middle. It is the only structure among the options with this property.

xxv) (d) Single ended queue
Explanation: Types of queues are: Priority Queue, Circular Queue, Ordinary (Linear) Queue, and Double Ended Queue (Deque). 'Single ended queue' is not a recognized type — a normal queue is simply called a linear queue, not single ended queue.

questions.question:
a) Define Primitive and Non-Primitive data structure with example. (3)
b) Define Linear and Non-linear data structure with example. (3)
c) Differentiate between data type and data structure. (2)
questions.answer:
a) Primitive and Non-Primitive Data Structures:

Primitive Data Structures:
Primitive data structures are the fundamental, basic data types that are directly supported by machine-level instructions and hold a single value at a time.

Examples:
1. Integer (int): Stores whole numbers. Example: 5, -10, 100
2. Float (float): Stores decimal numbers. Example: 3.14, -2.5
3. Character (char): Stores a single character. Example: 'A', 'z'
4. Boolean: Stores TRUE or FALSE.
5. Pointer: Stores a memory address.

Non-Primitive Data Structures:
Non-primitive data structures are derived from primitive data structures. They can store multiple values and represent complex relationships. They are user-defined and built using primitive types.

Classification:
1. Linear: Array, Stack, Queue, Linked List
2. Non-Linear: Tree, Graph

Examples:
- Array: A[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50} — stores multiple integers.
- Stack: A collection of elements with LIFO access.
- Tree: Hierarchical structure with parent-child nodes.

---

b) Linear and Non-Linear Data Structures:

Linear Data Structures:
A linear data structure is one in which data elements are arranged sequentially, one after another. Each element has a unique predecessor and successor (except first and last).

Characteristics:
1. Elements are stored in a sequential order.
2. Traversal is done in a single pass.
3. Memory is utilized sequentially.

Examples:
- Array: Elements stored in contiguous memory locations.
- Stack: LIFO structure — elements stacked one above another.
- Queue: FIFO structure — elements arranged in a line.
- Linked List: Elements connected via pointers in a chain.

Non-Linear Data Structures:
A non-linear data structure is one in which data elements are not arranged sequentially. An element can be connected to multiple elements (one-to-many or many-to-many relationships).

Characteristics:
1. Elements are arranged in a hierarchical or network manner.
2. Traversal requires special algorithms (DFS, BFS).
3. Data exists at multiple levels.

Examples:
- Tree: Hierarchical structure with root, internal nodes, and leaves.
- Graph: Network structure with vertices connected by edges.

---

c) Difference between Data Type and Data Structure:

1. Definition:
   Data Type: A classification that specifies what type of value a variable can hold and what operations can be performed on it.
   Data Structure: A way of organizing and storing a collection of data so that it can be accessed and manipulated efficiently.

2. Scope:
   Data Type: Deals with a single value at a time (e.g., int stores one integer).
   Data Structure: Deals with a collection of values and their relationships.

3. Implementation:
   Data Type: Implemented at language/compiler level (primitive types like int, float, char).
   Data Structure: Implemented by the programmer using data types (e.g., array of int, linked list of nodes).

4. Operations:
   Data Type: Operations are basic (arithmetic, comparison).
   Data Structure: Operations include insert, delete, search, traverse, sort.

5. Examples:
   Data Type: int, float, char, double.
   Data Structure: Array, Stack, Queue, Tree, Graph.

questions.question:
a) Write an algorithm for PUSH and POP operations on STACK using array. (4)
b) Convert the following infix expression into prefix expression:
(A - B/C) * (D*E - F) (4)
questions.answer:
a) PUSH and POP Algorithms for Stack using Array:

Variables:
- STACK[MAX]: Array of size MAX
- TOP: Pointer to top element (initialized to -1)
- MAX: Maximum stack size

PUSH Algorithm:
Algorithm: PUSH(STACK, TOP, MAX, ITEM)

Step 1: START
Step 2: If TOP = MAX - 1 then
           Print 'Stack Overflow — Stack is Full'
           EXIT
        End If
Step 3: Set TOP = TOP + 1
Step 4: Set STACK[TOP] = ITEM
Step 5: Print 'Element', ITEM, 'pushed successfully'
Step 6: STOP

POP Algorithm:
Algorithm: POP(STACK, TOP)

Step 1: START
Step 2: If TOP = -1 then
           Print 'Stack Underflow — Stack is Empty'
           EXIT
        End If
Step 3: Set ITEM = STACK[TOP]
Step 4: Set TOP = TOP - 1
Step 5: Print 'Element', ITEM, 'popped successfully'
Step 6: Return ITEM
Step 7: STOP

Example Trace:
MAX=5, Initially TOP=-1
PUSH(10): TOP=0, STACK=[10]
PUSH(20): TOP=1, STACK=[10,20]
PUSH(30): TOP=2, STACK=[10,20,30]
POP():    ITEM=30, TOP=1, STACK=[10,20]
POP():    ITEM=20, TOP=0, STACK=[10]

Time Complexity of both PUSH and POP: O(1)

---

b) Infix to Prefix Conversion of (A - B/C) * (D*E - F):

Rules for Infix to Prefix:
1. Reverse the infix expression.
2. Replace '(' with ')' and ')' with '('.
3. Apply infix to postfix algorithm on reversed expression.
4. Reverse the result to get prefix.

Operator Precedence (High to Low): *, / → +, -
Associativity: Left to Right (except for prefix conversion)

Method — Direct Step-by-Step:

Original: (A - B/C) * (D*E - F)

Step 1: Solve inside left bracket (A - B/C)
   B/C has higher precedence → B/C first → /BC
   A - /BC → -A/BC
   Left part prefix: -A/BC

Step 2: Solve inside right bracket (D*E - F)
   D*E has higher precedence → D*E first → *DE
   *DE - F → -*DEF
   Right part prefix: -*DEF

Step 3: Apply * between both parts:
   (-A/BC) * (-*DEF)
   → *-A/BC-*DEF

Prefix Expression: *-A/BC-*DEF

Verification:
*-A/BC-*DEF means:
   /BC = B/C
   -A/BC = A - B/C
   *DE = D*E
   -*DEF = D*E - F
   *-A/BC-*DEF = (A - B/C) * (D*E - F) ✓

questions.question:
a) What are circular queues? Write the algorithms one for inserting an element into a circular queue and other for deleting an element from a circular queue using arrays. (5)
b) What is a DeQueue? Explain its operation with example. (3)
questions.answer:
a) Circular Queue — Definition and Algorithms:

Definition:
A circular queue is a type of queue in which the last position is connected back to the first position, forming a circle. It solves the memory wastage problem of a linear queue by reusing the empty spaces left at the beginning after deletions.

The REAR pointer wraps around using: REAR = (REAR + 1) % MAX

Variables:
- QUEUE[MAX]: Array of size MAX
- FRONT: Index of front element (initialized to -1)
- REAR: Index of rear element (initialized to -1)

Insertion (ENQUEUE) Algorithm:
Algorithm: CQ_INSERT(QUEUE, FRONT, REAR, MAX, ITEM)

Step 1: START
Step 2: If FRONT = 0 AND REAR = MAX - 1 then
           Print 'Queue is Full'
           EXIT
        End If
Step 3: If (REAR + 1) % MAX = FRONT then
           Print 'Queue is Full (Circular)'
           EXIT
        End If
Step 4: If FRONT = -1 AND REAR = -1 then
           Set FRONT = 0
           Set REAR = 0
        Else
           Set REAR = (REAR + 1) % MAX
        End If
Step 5: Set QUEUE[REAR] = ITEM
Step 6: Print 'Element', ITEM, 'inserted'
Step 7: STOP

Deletion (DEQUEUE) Algorithm:
Algorithm: CQ_DELETE(QUEUE, FRONT, REAR)

Step 1: START
Step 2: If FRONT = -1 then
           Print 'Queue is Empty'
           EXIT
        End If
Step 3: Set ITEM = QUEUE[FRONT]
Step 4: If FRONT = REAR then
           (Last element deleted — reset to empty)
           Set FRONT = -1
           Set REAR = -1
        Else
           Set FRONT = (FRONT + 1) % MAX
        End If
Step 5: Print 'Element', ITEM, 'deleted'
Step 6: Return ITEM
Step 7: STOP

Example Trace (MAX=4):
Insert 10: F=0, R=0 → [10, _, _, _]
Insert 20: F=0, R=1 → [10,20, _, _]
Insert 30: F=0, R=2 → [10,20,30, _]
Delete:    F=1, R=2 → [_,20,30, _], ITEM=10
Insert 40: F=1, R=3 → [_,20,30,40]
Insert 50: R=(3+1)%4=0 → [50,20,30,40] (wraps!)

---

b) DeQueue (Double Ended Queue):

Definition:
A DeQueue (Double Ended Queue) is a linear data structure in which insertion and deletion of elements can be performed at BOTH ends — front and rear. It is a generalized form of both stack and queue.

Operations of DeQueue:
1. Insert at FRONT (Push Front)
2. Insert at REAR (Push Rear / Enqueue)
3. Delete from FRONT (Pop Front / Dequeue)
4. Delete from REAR (Pop Rear)
5. Peek at FRONT
6. Peek at REAR

Types:
1. Input Restricted DeQueue: Insertion only at REAR; deletion at both ends.
2. Output Restricted DeQueue: Deletion only at FRONT; insertion at both ends.

Example:
Initial DeQueue: [empty]
Insert 10 at REAR:  [10]
Insert 20 at REAR:  [10, 20]
Insert 5 at FRONT:  [5, 10, 20]
Delete from FRONT:  [10, 20] → returns 5
Delete from REAR:   [10] → returns 20
Insert 30 at FRONT: [30, 10]

Applications:
1. Palindrome checking.
2. Implementing both stack and queue.
3. Sliding window maximum problems.
4. Browser history (forward and backward navigation).

questions.question:
a) Define the following terms, with examples:
i) Header linked list ii) Circular linked list (2 + 2)
b) Write an algorithm to insert a node at the beginning of a single linked list. (4)
questions.answer:
a) i) Header Linked List:

Definition:
A header linked list is a special type of linked list that always contains a special node at the very beginning called the header node (or dummy node). This header node does not store actual data — it serves as a sentinel that simplifies list operations.

Types of Header Linked Lists:
1. Grounded Header List: The last node points to NULL.
   Structure: [HEADER|→] → [D1|→] → [D2|→] → ... → [Dn|NULL]

2. Circular Header List: The last node points back to the header node.
   Structure: [HEADER|→] → [D1|→] → [D2|→] → ... → [Dn|→HEADER]

Advantages:
- Simplifies insertion and deletion at the beginning.
- The list is never truly 'empty' — the header node always exists.
- Header node can store metadata like count of nodes.

Example:
For list with values 10, 20, 30:
[HEADER(0)|→] → [10|→] → [20|→] → [30|NULL]

---

a) ii) Circular Linked List:

Definition:
A circular linked list is a linked list in which the NEXT pointer of the last node points back to the FIRST node of the list, forming a circle. There is no NULL pointer in the list.

Types:
1. Circular Singly Linked List: Each node has one NEXT pointer; last node points to first.
2. Circular Doubly Linked List: Each node has NEXT and PREV; last points to first, first's PREV points to last.

Diagram:
[10|→] → [20|→] → [30|→] → [40|→]
  ↑_________________________________|

Advantages:
1. No NULL in any node — simplifies traversal.
2. Can start traversal from any node.
3. Efficient for circular/round-robin applications.
4. Efficient implementation of queue (insertion at rear, deletion at front).

Applications: CPU scheduling (Round Robin), circular buffer, media players (repeat mode).

Example: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → (back to 10)

---

b) Algorithm to Insert a Node at the Beginning of a Singly Linked List:

Algorithm: INSERT_BEGINNING(HEAD, NEW_DATA)

Step 1: START
Step 2: Create a new node NEW_NODE
Step 3: Set NEW_NODE -> DATA = NEW_DATA
Step 4: If HEAD = NULL then
           (List is empty)
           Set NEW_NODE -> NEXT = NULL
           Set HEAD = NEW_NODE
           Print 'First node inserted'
           STOP
        End If
Step 5: Set NEW_NODE -> NEXT = HEAD
        (New node now points to old first node)
Step 6: Set HEAD = NEW_NODE
        (HEAD now points to new node)
Step 7: Print 'Node with data', NEW_DATA, 'inserted at beginning'
Step 8: STOP

Explanation:
- A new node is created and its data is set.
- The new node's NEXT pointer is set to the current HEAD (old first node).
- HEAD is updated to point to the new node.
- This makes the new node the new first node of the list.

Example:
Before: HEAD → [20] → [30] → [40] → NULL
Insert 10 at beginning:
Step 5: NEW_NODE(10) -> NEXT = HEAD(20)
Step 6: HEAD = NEW_NODE(10)
After:  HEAD → [10] → [20] → [30] → [40] → NULL

Time Complexity: O(1) — no traversal needed.
Space Complexity: O(1) — only one new node created.

questions.question:
a) Construct a binary tree wherein-order and pre-order traversals of the binary tree produce following sequences.
In-Order: 7, 9, 4, 2, 5, 1, 3, 6, 8
Pre-Order: 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 5, 3, 6, 8 (4)

b) What is a Binary Search Tree (BST)? Show the structure of the binary search tree after adding each of the following values in that order: 10, 25, 2, 4, 7, 13, 11, 22. What is the height of the created binary search tree? (4)
questions.answer:
a) Construct Binary Tree from In-order and Pre-order:

Given:
In-order:  7, 9, 4, 2, 5, 1, 3, 6, 8
Pre-order: 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 5, 3, 6, 8

Rule: First element of Pre-order = Root.
In In-order: elements LEFT of root = Left Subtree; elements RIGHT of root = Right Subtree.

Step 1:
Root = 1 (first of Pre-order)
In-order: [7,9,4,2,5] | 1 | [3,6,8]
Left subtree In-order:  7, 9, 4, 2, 5
Right subtree In-order: 3, 6, 8
Left subtree Pre-order:  2, 4, 7, 9, 5
Right subtree Pre-order: 3, 6, 8

Step 2: Left Subtree (In: 7,9,4,2,5 | Pre: 2,4,7,9,5)
Root = 2
In-order: [7,9,4] | 2 | [5]
Left of 2: 7,9,4  Right of 2: 5
Left Pre-order: 4,7,9   Right Pre-order: 5

Step 3: Sub-Left (In: 7,9,4 | Pre: 4,7,9)
Root = 4
In-order: [7,9] | 4
Left of 4: 7,9   Right of 4: empty
Left Pre-order: 7,9
Root = 7, Right of 7 = 9

Step 4: Right Subtree of Root 1 (In: 3,6,8 | Pre: 3,6,8)
Root = 3
In-order: | 3 | [6,8]
Right of 3: 6,8
Right Pre-order: 6,8
Root = 6, Right of 6 = 8

Final Binary Tree Structure:
              1
            /   \
           2     3
          / \     \
         4   5     6
        /             \
       7               8
        \
         9

---

b) Binary Search Tree (BST) — Definition and Construction:

Definition:
A Binary Search Tree is a binary tree where for every node N:
- All values in the LEFT subtree < N's value
- All values in the RIGHT subtree > N's value
- Both left and right subtrees are also BSTs

Construction by inserting: 10, 25, 2, 4, 7, 13, 11, 22

Insert 10: Root = 10
    10

Insert 25: 25 > 10 → Right of 10
    10
      \
      25

Insert 2: 2 < 10 → Left of 10
    10
   /  \
  2   25

Insert 4: 4 < 10 → Left; 4 > 2 → Right of 2
    10
   /  \
  2   25
   \
    4

Insert 7: 7 < 10 → Left; 7 > 2 → Right of 2; 7 > 4 → Right of 4
    10
   /  \
  2   25
   \
    4
     \
      7

Insert 13: 13 > 10 → Right; 13 < 25 → Left of 25
    10
   /  \
  2   25
   \ /
   4 13
    \
     7

Insert 11: 11 > 10 → Right; 11 < 25 → Left of 25; 11 < 13 → Left of 13
    10
   /  \
  2   25
   \ /
   4 13
    \  /
     7 11

Insert 22: 22 > 10 → Right; 22 < 25 → Left of 25; 22 > 13 → Right of 13
    10
   /  \
  2   25
   \ /
   4 13
    \ / \
    7 11 22

Final BST:
          10
         /  \
        2    25
         \  /
          4 13
           \ / \
            7 11 22

Height of BST:
Height = number of edges on longest root-to-leaf path.
Path: 10 → 25 → 13 → 11 or 10 → 25 → 13 → 22 → length = 3 edges
Path: 10 → 2 → 4 → 7 → length = 3 edges

Height of the BST = 3

questions.question: Write algorithm for Breadth First Search (BFS) and give the complexity. (6 + 2)
questions.answer:
Breadth First Search (BFS):

Definition:
BFS is a graph traversal algorithm that explores all vertices of a graph level by level, starting from a given source vertex. It visits all neighbours of a vertex before moving to the next level of vertices.

Data Structure Used: QUEUE (FIFO)

Key Terms:
- Visited[]: Boolean array to track visited vertices.
- Queue: Used to store vertices to be explored.

Algorithm: BFS(GRAPH, START)

Step 1: START
Step 2: Initialize all vertices as NOT VISITED.
        Set VISITED[v] = FALSE for all vertices v.
Step 3: Create an empty QUEUE Q.
Step 4: Mark START as visited: VISITED[START] = TRUE
Step 5: Enqueue START into Q: ENQUEUE(Q, START)
Step 6: Repeat while Q is not empty:
   Step 6a: VERTEX = DEQUEUE(Q)
            Print VERTEX  (Visit/Process the vertex)
   Step 6b: For each adjacent vertex ADJ of VERTEX do:
               If VISITED[ADJ] = FALSE then
                  Set VISITED[ADJ] = TRUE
                  ENQUEUE(Q, ADJ)
               End If
            End For
        End While
Step 7: STOP

Example:
Graph (Adjacency List):
0 → [1, 2]
1 → [0, 3, 4]
2 → [0, 5]
3 → [1]
4 → [1]
5 → [2]

BFS from vertex 0:
Step 1: Visit 0, Queue: [0]
Step 2: Dequeue 0, Visit neighbours 1,2
        Queue: [1, 2], Visited: 0,1,2
Step 3: Dequeue 1, Visit neighbours 3,4 (0 already visited)
        Queue: [2, 3, 4], Visited: 0,1,2,3,4
Step 4: Dequeue 2, Visit neighbour 5 (0 already visited)
        Queue: [3, 4, 5], Visited: 0,1,2,3,4,5
Step 5: Dequeue 3 — no unvisited neighbours
Step 6: Dequeue 4 — no unvisited neighbours
Step 7: Dequeue 5 — no unvisited neighbours
        Queue empty — STOP

BFS Order: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

Properties of BFS:
1. Visits all vertices reachable from source.
2. Finds shortest path (in terms of number of edges) from source to all other vertices.
3. Produces a BFS tree (spanning tree).

Complexity Analysis:

Time Complexity:
- Adjacency List representation: O(V + E)
  Each vertex is enqueued and dequeued exactly once: O(V)
  Each edge is examined exactly twice (once from each endpoint): O(E)
  Total: O(V + E)

- Adjacency Matrix representation: O(V²)
  For each vertex, we scan the entire row to find neighbours: O(V) per vertex
  Total for V vertices: O(V²)

Space Complexity:
- O(V) for the visited array.
- O(V) for the queue (at most V vertices in queue at once).
- Total Space: O(V)

Applications of BFS:
1. Finding shortest path in unweighted graphs.
2. Level-order traversal of trees.
3. Finding all connected components.
4. Web crawlers.
5. Social network friend suggestion (people within k connections).

b) B-Tree of Order m:

Definition:
A B-tree of order m (also called degree m) is a self-balancing multi-way search tree that satisfies the following properties:

1. Every node has at most m children.
2. Every non-leaf node (except root) has at least ⌈m/2⌉ children.
3. The root has at least 2 children if it is not a leaf.
4. All leaf nodes appear at the same level (the tree is perfectly height-balanced).
5. A non-leaf node with k children contains exactly k-1 keys.
6. All keys within a node are sorted in ascending order.

Example B-tree of order 3 (2-3 tree):
- Each node can have 1 or 2 keys.
- Each node can have 2 or 3 children.

Structure:
       [20 | 40]
      /    |    \
  [10]  [30]  [50|60]

When is B-tree preferred:
1. Database Indexing: B-trees are preferred for large disk-based databases where data is stored on secondary storage (hard disk). They minimize disk I/O operations because a single node can hold many keys.
2. File Systems: Used in file systems (e.g., NTFS, ext4) for directory indexing.
3. Large Data: When data is too large to fit in main memory.
4. Multi-level Indexing: Efficient for range queries — find all keys between k1 and k2.
5. Balanced Performance: Guarantees O(log n) for search, insert, delete regardless of input order.
6. External Sorting: Preferred over AVL trees for external storage access due to larger node size reducing tree height.

questions.question:
a) Write a recursive function to calculate the GCD of two numbers. (4)
b) Write an algorithm to evaluate a postfix expression. (4)
questions.answer:
a) Recursive Function to Calculate GCD:

GCD (Greatest Common Divisor) is the largest number that divides both given numbers without leaving a remainder.

Mathematical Recurrence (Euclidean Algorithm):
GCD(a, b) = a,          if b = 0
GCD(a, b) = GCD(b, a mod b),  if b ≠ 0

Algorithm: GCD(A, B)

Step 1: If B = 0 then
           Return A  (Base case)
        End If
Step 2: Return GCD(B, A mod B)  (Recursive case)

Pseudocode:
function GCD(A, B):
    if B = 0:
        return A
    else:
        return GCD(B, A mod B)

C-like code:
int GCD(int a, int b) {
    if (b == 0)
        return a;       // base case
    return GCD(b, a % b);  // recursive call
}

Example Trace: GCD(48, 18)
GCD(48, 18) = GCD(18, 48 mod 18) = GCD(18, 12)
GCD(18, 12) = GCD(12, 18 mod 12) = GCD(12, 6)
GCD(12, 6)  = GCD(6, 12 mod 6)  = GCD(6, 0)
GCD(6, 0)   = 6  (base case: b=0, return a=6)

Result: GCD(48, 18) = 6

Time Complexity: O(log(min(a,b))) — same as iterative Euclidean algorithm.
Space Complexity: O(log(min(a,b))) — for recursive call stack.

---

b) Algorithm to Evaluate a Postfix Expression:

Postfix (Reverse Polish Notation) evaluation uses a Stack.
Rule:
- If token is OPERAND → PUSH onto stack.
- If token is OPERATOR → POP two operands, apply operator, PUSH result.

Algorithm: EVALUATE_POSTFIX(EXPRESSION)

Step 1: START
Step 2: Create an empty STACK S
Step 3: Scan EXPRESSION from LEFT to RIGHT, token by token:

        Repeat for each TOKEN in EXPRESSION:

           If TOKEN is an OPERAND (number) then
              PUSH(S, TOKEN)

           Else if TOKEN is an OPERATOR (+, -, *, /) then
              If stack has fewer than 2 elements then
                 Print 'Invalid Expression'
                 EXIT
              End If
              POP(S) → OPERAND2
              POP(S) → OPERAND1
              Compute RESULT = OPERAND1 OPERATOR OPERAND2
              PUSH(S, RESULT)

           End If
        End Repeat

Step 4: POP(S) → FINAL_RESULT
Step 5: If S is empty then
           Print 'Result =', FINAL_RESULT
        Else
           Print 'Invalid Expression'
        End If
Step 6: STOP

Example: Evaluate postfix 5 3 2 * + 8 -

Token | Action                          | Stack
-------------------------------------------------
5     | Push 5                          | [5]
3     | Push 3                          | [5, 3]
2     | Push 2                          | [5, 3, 2]
*     | Pop 2,3 → 3*2=6, Push 6        | [5, 6]
+     | Pop 6,5 → 5+6=11, Push 11      | [11]
8     | Push 8                          | [11, 8]
-     | Pop 8,11 → 11-8=3, Push 3      | [3]

Final Result = 3

Time Complexity: O(n) — each token is processed exactly once.
Space Complexity: O(n) — stack holds at most n/2 operands.

questions.question:
a) Write short notes on: i) ADT ii) Threaded Binary Tree (2 + 2)
b) Write the in-order, pre-order and post-order traversal of the following binary tree. (4)
[Binary tree diagram with nodes as given in the paper]
questions.answer:
a) i) ADT (Abstract Data Type):

Definition:
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a mathematical model for data types defined by its behavior (operations) from the user's perspective, without specifying how the operations are implemented internally.

Key Concepts:
1. ADT describes WHAT operations can be performed, not HOW they are implemented.
2. It provides data abstraction — implementation details are hidden.
3. Users interact with ADT through a well-defined interface.

Example — Stack ADT:
Data: A collection of elements with LIFO access.
Operations:
  - push(x): Insert x at top.
  - pop(): Remove and return top element.
  - peek(): Return top without removing.
  - isEmpty(): Check if stack is empty.
The user does not need to know if the stack is implemented using array or linked list.

Benefits:
1. Promotes modularity and code reuse.
2. Implementation can change without affecting users.
3. Simplifies complex system design.

---

a) ii) Threaded Binary Tree:

Definition:
A Threaded Binary Tree is a binary tree in which the NULL pointers (which are normally wasted) are replaced by threads — pointers to the in-order predecessor or in-order successor of the node.

Purpose:
To allow efficient inorder traversal without using a stack or recursion.

Types:
1. Single Threaded Tree: Only right NULL pointers are replaced by threads to in-order successor.
2. Double Threaded Tree: Both left and right NULL pointers are replaced — left threads point to in-order predecessor, right threads point to in-order successor.

Thread vs. Normal Pointer:
- A boolean field (RTHREAD, LTHREAD) in each node indicates whether the pointer is a normal link (child) or a thread.

Advantage:
- Inorder traversal is O(n) with O(1) extra space — no recursion stack needed.
- Efficient in memory-constrained environments.

Example:
For tree: A → B (left), C (right); B → D (left)
In inorder: D, B, A, C
D's right NULL → thread to B (inorder successor)
B's right → normal pointer to A... and so on.

---

b) Tree Traversals:

Note: Since the actual binary tree diagram from the exam paper is not available, a standard example binary tree is used to demonstrate all three traversals.

Example Binary Tree:
            1
           / \
          2   3
         / \ / \
        4  5 6  7

In-order Traversal (Left → Root → Right):
Visit: 4, 2, 5, 1, 6, 3, 7

Pre-order Traversal (Root → Left → Right):
Visit: 1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 6, 7

Post-order Traversal (Left → Right → Root):
Visit: 4, 5, 2, 6, 7, 3, 1

Rules Summary:
- Pre-order:  ROOT first, then left subtree, then right subtree.
- In-order:   Left subtree first, then ROOT, then right subtree.
- Post-order: Left subtree first, then right subtree, then ROOT last.

Time Complexity of all traversals: O(n)
Space Complexity: O(h) where h = height of tree (for recursive call stack).

questions.question:
Which is/are the application(s) of stack?
(a) Function calls (b) Large number Arithmetic (c) Evaluation of arithmetic expressions (d) All of the above
questions.answer:
Answer: (d) All of the above

Explanation — Applications of Stack:

1. Function Calls:
   When a function is called, the system saves the return address, local variables, and parameters on the call stack. When the function returns, these are popped off the stack. This is why recursion uses the stack — each recursive call pushes a new frame.

2. Large Number Arithmetic:
   Very large numbers (beyond the range of standard data types) can be stored digit by digit in a stack. Arithmetic operations like addition and multiplication are performed using stack-based algorithms.

3. Evaluation of Arithmetic Expressions:
   Postfix (Reverse Polish Notation) expressions are evaluated using a stack:
   - Operands are pushed onto the stack.
   - When an operator is encountered, two operands are popped, the operation is performed, and the result is pushed back.

Other Applications of Stack:
4. Infix to Postfix/Prefix conversion.
5. Undo/Redo operations in text editors.
6. Balanced parentheses checking.
7. Backtracking algorithms (DFS, maze solving).
8. Browser back/forward navigation.

questions.question:
In Binary trees nodes with no successor are called -
(a) End nodes (b) Final nodes (c) Last nodes (d) Terminal nodes
questions.answer:
Answer: (d) Terminal nodes

Explanation:
In a binary tree, nodes that have NO children (no left child and no right child) are called terminal nodes. They are also known as leaf nodes or external nodes.

Key Properties of Terminal Nodes:
1. Their degree is 0 — they have no successors.
2. They appear at the lowest levels of the tree.
3. Both left and right child pointers are NULL.
4. In a full binary tree with I internal nodes, the number of terminal nodes L = I + 1.

Example:
       A
      / \
     B   C
    / \
   D   E

Terminal nodes: D, E, C — they have no children.
Non-terminal (internal) nodes: A, B — they have children.

questions.question:
The data structure required for Breadth First Search on a graph is -
(a) queue (b) stack (c) array (d) None of the above
questions.answer:
Answer: (a) queue

Explanation:
Breadth First Search (BFS) uses a Queue (FIFO) data structure to traverse a graph level by level.

Why Queue?
- BFS explores all neighbours of a vertex before moving to the next level.
- When a vertex is visited, all its unvisited neighbours are added to the queue.
- The queue ensures that vertices are processed in the order they were discovered (FIFO).
- This guarantees that closer vertices (shorter path from source) are processed before farther vertices.

Working Principle:
1. Start: Enqueue the source vertex and mark it visited.
2. Dequeue a vertex, process it.
3. Enqueue all its unvisited neighbours and mark them visited.
4. Repeat until queue is empty.

Contrast: DFS (Depth First Search) uses a STACK (or recursion, which implicitly uses the call stack).

questions.question:
The data structure required to evaluate a postfix expression is -
(a) queue (b) stack (c) linked-list (d) All of the above
questions.answer:
Answer: (b) stack

Explanation:
A Stack is the data structure used to evaluate a postfix (Reverse Polish Notation) expression.

Why Stack?
Stack follows LIFO (Last In First Out), which is ideal for postfix evaluation because:
1. When an operand is encountered → PUSH it onto the stack.
2. When an operator is encountered → POP the top two operands, apply the operator, and PUSH the result back.
3. At the end, the stack contains exactly one element — the final result.

Example: Evaluate 4 5 + 2 *
Token 4 → Push → Stack: [4]
Token 5 → Push → Stack: [4, 5]
Token + → Pop 5,4 → 4+5=9, Push → Stack: [9]
Token 2 → Push → Stack: [9, 2]
Token * → Pop 2,9 → 9*2=18, Push → Stack: [18]
Result = 18

Time Complexity: O(n) — each token processed once.
Space Complexity: O(n) — for the stack.

questions.question:
A linear collection of data elements where the linear node is given by means of pointer is called -
(a) Linked list (b) node list (c) primitive list (d) None of these
questions.answer:
Answer: (a) Linked list

Explanation:
A Linked List is a linear collection of data elements (called nodes) where the order of elements is determined by pointers. Each node contains:
1. DATA field: Stores the actual data value.
2. NEXT field: A pointer that stores the address of the next node.

The linear order in a linked list is established by means of pointers (not by physical/contiguous memory location like arrays).

Diagram:
[10|→] → [20|→] → [30|→] → [40|NULL]
HEAD

Types of Linked Lists:
1. Singly Linked List: Each node has one NEXT pointer.
2. Doubly Linked List: Each node has PREV and NEXT pointers.
3. Circular Linked List: Last node's NEXT points to first node.

Key Difference from Array:
- Array: Linear order by contiguous memory (index-based).
- Linked List: Linear order by pointers (pointer-based).

questions.question:
For an undirected graph with n vertices and e edges, the sum of the degree of each vertex is equal to -
(a) 2n (b) 2e (c) (e²+1)/2 (d) (2n-1)/2
questions.answer:
Answer: (b) 2e

Explanation — Handshaking Lemma:
For any undirected graph with n vertices and e edges:
Sum of degrees of all vertices = 2e

Proof:
- In an undirected graph, every edge (u, v) connects two vertices: u and v.
- This edge contributes 1 to the degree of vertex u AND 1 to the degree of vertex v.
- Therefore, each edge contributes exactly 2 to the total sum of degrees.
- With e edges total: Sum of all degrees = 2 × e = 2e.

This result is known as the Handshaking Lemma (or Degree Sum Formula).

Consequence: The number of vertices with odd degree is always even.

Example:
Graph with 4 vertices and edges: (A-B), (B-C), (C-D), (A-D), (A-C)
e = 5 edges
deg(A)=3, deg(B)=2, deg(C)=3, deg(D)=2
Sum = 3+2+3+2 = 10 = 2×5 = 2e ✓

questions.question:
When new data are to be inserted into a data structure, but there is not available space; this situation is usually called -
(a) Overflow (b) Underflow (c) houseful (d) memory full
questions.answer:
Answer: (a) Overflow

Explanation:
Overflow is the error condition that occurs when an attempt is made to insert (add) a new element into a data structure that is already FULL — there is no available space to accommodate the new data.

Examples of Overflow:
1. Stack Overflow: Attempting PUSH on a full stack (TOP = MAX-1).
2. Queue Overflow: Attempting ENQUEUE on a full queue (REAR = MAX-1 for linear queue).
3. Array Overflow: Trying to add an element beyond the declared array size.

Action taken on Overflow:
- Print error message 'Overflow'.
- Return or exit without inserting.

Opposite — Underflow:
- Underflow occurs when deletion is attempted on an EMPTY data structure.
- Example: POP on empty stack (TOP=-1), DEQUEUE on empty queue (FRONT=-1).

questions.question:
A data structure where elements can be added or removed at either end but not in the middle is called -
(a) Stacks (b) queues (c) dequeue (d) linked lists
questions.answer:
Answer: (c) dequeue

Explanation:
A Deque (Double Ended Queue) is a linear data structure that allows insertion and deletion at BOTH ends — the FRONT and the REAR — but NOT in the middle.

Deque Operations:
1. Insert at FRONT
2. Insert at REAR
3. Delete from FRONT
4. Delete from REAR

Why not the others:
- Stack: Insertion and deletion only at ONE end (TOP). Not both ends.
- Queue: Insertion only at REAR; deletion only at FRONT. Restricted to one end each.
- Linked List: Insertion and deletion possible at any position including middle — does not restrict to ends only.

Types of Deque:
1. Input Restricted: Insert only at REAR; delete from both ends.
2. Output Restricted: Delete only from FRONT; insert at both ends.

Applications:
1. Palindrome checking.
2. Sliding window algorithms.
3. Implementing both Stack and Queue using a single structure.

questions.question:
The post-order traversal of a binary tree is DEBFCA. Find out the pre-order traversal -
(a) ABFCDE (b) ADBFEC (c) ABDECF (d) ABDCEF
questions.answer:
Answer: (c) ABDECF

Explanation:
Post-order traversal visits: Left → Right → Root
So the LAST element in post-order is always the ROOT.

Given Post-order: D E B F C A
Root = A (last element)

Now, in post-order, before A we have: D E B F C
We need to identify left and right subtrees.

Since it is a binary tree and post-order of right subtree ends just before root:
Looking at the structure:
- Right subtree post-order ends with C → Root of right = C
- Left subtree: D E B → Root of left = B (last of left group)

Left subtree post-order: D E B
  Root = B
  Left of B: D (single node)
  Right of B: E (single node)

Right subtree post-order: F C
  Root = C
  Left of C: F (single node)

Tree Structure:
       A
      / \
     B   C
    / \ /
   D  E F

Pre-order (Root → Left → Right):
A → B → D → E → C → F
Pre-order = ABDECF ✓

Answer: (c) ABDECF

questions.question:
A full binary tree with n leaves contains -
(a) n - 1 nodes (b) log₂ n nodes (c) 2n - 1 nodes (d) 2ⁿ nodes
questions.answer:
Answer: (c) 2n - 1 nodes

Explanation:
In a full binary tree (where every internal node has exactly 2 children):
- Let L = number of leaf nodes = n
- Let I = number of internal nodes

Property of full binary tree: L = I + 1
Therefore: I = L - 1 = n - 1

Total nodes = Leaf nodes + Internal nodes
Total nodes = n + (n - 1) = 2n - 1

Verification with example:
Full binary tree with 4 leaves:
       A          ← internal
      / \
     B   C        ← internal nodes
    / \ / \
   D  E F  G     ← 4 leaf nodes

Leaves (L) = 4 = n
Internal nodes (I) = 3 = n - 1
Total = 4 + 3 = 7 = 2(4) - 1 = 2n - 1 ✓

questions.question:
Which of the following data structure is nonlinear type?
(a) Graph (b) Stacks (c) Lists (d) None of the above
questions.answer:
Answer: (a) Graph

Explanation:
A Graph is a non-linear data structure because its elements (vertices/nodes) are not arranged in a sequential order. A vertex in a graph can be connected to multiple other vertices through edges, creating complex many-to-many relationships across multiple levels.

Why the others are Linear:
- Stacks: Linear — elements are arranged sequentially with LIFO access at one end.
- Lists (Linked Lists): Linear — elements are connected in a sequential chain via pointers.

Non-linear Data Structures:
1. Tree: Hierarchical (one-to-many) relationships between nodes.
2. Graph: Network (many-to-many) relationships between vertices.

Key Feature of Non-linear Structures:
- Cannot be traversed in a single linear pass.
- Require special algorithms like BFS and DFS for traversal.
- Data exists at multiple levels or in a network.

questions.question:
Which of the following is not the type of queue?
(a) Priority queue (b) Circular queue (c) Ordinary queue (d) Single ended queue
questions.answer:
Answer: (d) Single ended queue

Explanation:
The recognized types of queues in data structures are:

1. Ordinary Queue (Linear Queue):
   - Simple FIFO queue.
   - Insertion at REAR, deletion at FRONT.

2. Circular Queue:
   - Rear wraps around to front using modulo operation.
   - Solves memory wastage of linear queue.

3. Priority Queue:
   - Each element has a priority.
   - Element with highest priority is dequeued first.
   - Types: Ascending (Min) and Descending (Max) priority queue.

4. Double Ended Queue (Deque):
   - Insertion and deletion at both ends.

'Single ended queue' is NOT a standard recognized type of queue in data structures.
A normal/ordinary queue is sometimes informally called a queue, but never a 'single ended queue' as a formal classification.

Note: If anything, a 'single ended' structure would describe a Stack (only one end for both insert and delete), not a queue.
